title: Social Impacts of ICT
part: Part C — Software and ICT in Life

blocks.html: After studying this chapter you will be able to:

items.html: list the positive and negative effects of ICT on society
explain the digital divide and steps to reduce it
identify common cyber crimes and types of malware, and protect yourself from them
name the main Indian cyber laws
explain intellectual property, plagiarism and software licences
practise netiquette, protect your digital footprint and use devices in a healthy way
handle e-waste responsibly

blocks.html: Every powerful tool can be used well or badly. A knife cuts vegetables and can also hurt. ICT is the same: it has made life easier in countless ways, but it has also brought new problems.

blocks.caption: Figure 9.1 · Benefits and risks of ICT

items.html: Communication — calls, messages and video chats connect families across cities and countries at almost no cost.
Education — free lessons, e-books and courses reach students everywhere.
Employment — new jobs in IT, digital marketing, data entry, app development and online services; work from home.
Governance — faster, transparent services with less corruption (DBT, online certificates).
Health — telemedicine and digital records save lives and travel.
Financial inclusion — UPI and Jan Dhan accounts brought banking to crores of people.
Environment — less paper and less travel when work is done online.
Cyber crime — fraud, hacking and identity theft.
Privacy loss — personal data collected by apps and websites can be misused.
Health problems — eye strain, poor posture, lack of sleep and exercise.
Addiction — excessive gaming, scrolling and social media.
Fake news and misinformation — rumours spread quickly and can cause panic or violence.
Cyberbullying — insulting, threatening or shaming someone online.
Job changes — automation replaces some routine jobs.
E-waste — discarded devices pollute soil and water.
Digital divide — those without devices or skills are left behind.

blocks.html: The digital divide is the gap between people who have access to computers, the internet and digital skills and those who do not.
It appears between:

items.html: urban and rural areas,
rich and poor families,
men and women,
young and old people,
people who know English and those who do not.

blocks.text: Steps to bridge it in India:

items.html: BharatNet — optical fibre to gram panchayats.
Common Service Centres (CSCs) — village centres offering digital services.
PMGDISHA (Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan) — digital literacy training for rural citizens.
Cheaper smartphones and data, and apps in Indian languages.
Computer labs and smart classes in government schools.

blocks.html: Cyber crime is any crime in which a computer, phone or network is used as a tool or a target.

rows: Breaking into a computer or account without permission
Fake messages or sites that steal passwords and bank details
Check sender and URL; never click unknown links
Using someone's personal details to cheat others
Do not share Aadhaar, PAN or photos carelessly
"You have won a prize, pay a fee", fake customer care, fake job offers
Never share OTP/PIN; use only official apps and numbers
Harassing, insulting or threatening someone online
Do not reply; block, save evidence, tell a trusted adult, report
Repeatedly following and threatening someone online
Attaches itself to a file and spreads when the file is shared and opened
Spreads by itself across networks without needing a file
Looks like a useful program but does harm in the background
Secretly records what you do and steals information
Locks your files and demands money to unlock them

blocks.html: Protection: install a good antivirus and keep it updated, keep Windows and apps updated, download only from official stores, scan pen drives, take regular backups, and do not open unknown attachments.

items.html: Call the national cyber crime helpline 1930 immediately (especially for money fraud — the sooner, the better the chance of stopping the payment).
Report at cybercrime.gov.in.
Inform your bank and change your passwords.
Keep screenshots and messages as evidence.

Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended in 2008) — India's main cyber law. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, and defines punishments for hacking, identity theft, sending offensive messages and publishing obscene material.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — protects people's personal data and says how companies may collect and use it.
Cyber crimes can be reported at police cyber cells in every state.

blocks.html: Intellectual property (IP) is a creation of the mind — a book, song, film, design, invention, logo or software. The law protects it.

rows: The name and logo of a company

items.html: Plagiarism — copying someone else's work or ideas and presenting them as your own. Always give credit to the source.
Software piracy — using or distributing software without a valid licence. It is illegal.

rows: Must be bought; source code is secret
Free to use, but code is not open
Some media players and PDF readers
Free to try for a limited time, then must be bought
Free to use, study, change and share

blocks.html: Creative Commons licences let creators share their work with others under simple conditions, such as giving credit.
Netiquette means good manners on the internet.

items.html: Be polite and respectful; do not use abusive language.
Do not type in ALL CAPITALS — it looks like shouting.
Do not share other people's photos or information without permission.
Check facts before forwarding a message.
Respect copyright; give credit.
Do not spam people with unnecessary messages.

blocks.html: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online — posts, photos, comments, searches and likes. It can be seen by colleges and employers years later. Think before you post.
Ergonomics is the study of arranging the work place to suit the human body.

items.html: Eye strain — follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Keep the screen at arm's length, slightly below eye level.
Posture — sit straight with your back supported and feet flat on the floor.
Repetitive strain injury (RSI) — pain in the wrists and fingers from long typing; keep wrists straight and take breaks.
Sleep — avoid screens for an hour before bedtime.
Screen addiction — set time limits, keep phone-free meals and spend time outdoors.

blocks.html: E-waste is discarded electronic equipment — old phones, computers, chargers, batteries and TVs. India is one of the largest producers of e-waste in the world.
E-waste contains harmful substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium. Burning or dumping it pollutes air, soil and water and harms health. It also contains valuable metals that can be recovered.

items.html: Reduce — use devices for longer; repair instead of replacing.
Reuse — donate working devices to schools or NGOs.
Recycle — give e-waste only to authorised recyclers or company take-back schemes, as required by India's E-Waste (Management) Rules.
Never throw batteries or e-waste with household garbage.

blocks.html: Green computing means using computers in an environment-friendly way: switch off devices when not in use, use power-saving modes, print only when necessary and print on both sides.
Did you know? The metals in about one tonne of discarded mobile phones contain more gold than one tonne of gold ore — which is why proper recycling matters.

lessons.title: Workshop 9: Be a smart digital citizen

blocks.html: Aim: To practise safe, ethical and healthy use of ICT.

items.html: Password test. Write three example passwords (not your real ones). Rate each as weak, medium or strong and explain why. Create a strong passphrase such as Litti- Chokha#Patna2026!.
Spot the scam. Your teacher will display five messages (lottery win, KYC update, job offer, bank alert, school notice). Classify each as genuine or fraud with reasons.
Digital footprint audit. Search your own name online (with a parent). Note what appears. List three things you would not want a future employer to see.
Ergonomics check. Sit at a lab computer and check: screen distance, screen height, chair height, wrist position, lighting. Fix anything wrong.
E-waste survey. Count the unused electronic items in your home (old phones, chargers, cables). Find the nearest authorised collection point.

blocks.html: Record: Make a "Cyber Safety Pledge" of ten points and sign it.

items.html: ICT has positive effects (communication, education, jobs, governance, health, inclusion) and negative effects (cyber crime, privacy loss, health problems, addiction, fake news, e-waste).
The digital divide is the gap in access and skills; BharatNet, CSCs and PMGDISHA help bridge it.
Cyber crimes include hacking, phishing, identity theft, fraud, cyberbullying and piracy. Malware includes viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware.
Report cyber crime on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in. India's main cyber law is the IT Act, 2000; personal data is protected by the DPDP Act, 2023.
Copyright, patents and trademarks protect intellectual property; plagiarism and piracy are wrong.
Follow netiquette, guard your digital footprint, use the 20-20-20 rule and recycle e- waste responsibly.

blocks.html: footprint. How can a student become a responsible digital citizen?

items.html: Cyber safety assembly: In a group, prepare a 10-minute skit on an online fraud and how it was stopped by calling 1930. Perform it in the school assembly.
E-waste collection drive: Organise an e-waste collection box in your school for one month. Record what was collected and hand it to an authorised recycler.
Healthy screen-time plan: Track your daily screen time for one week. Prepare a chart and a personal plan to reduce it by 25%.
